claims.text: Adding approximately 1–2 wt% Ti during reactive spark plasma sintering will cause localized alloying at W/Cu interfaces.
Localized interfacial alloying will form a graded W/Cu interphase.
The graded interphase will minimize voids and phase separation.
The Ti-modified composite will maintain mechanical durability under fusion-reactor irradiation conditions.
The proposed starting material is a W-particle or interconnected-W-skeleton composite embedded in a Cu matrix.
Ti will be incorporated into a mechanically alloyed W-Cu powder mixture before reactive spark plasma sintering.
Processing above the Cu melting point but below the W melting point will leave Cu molten while W remains solid.
Ti reacts preferentially at the W/Cu interface during reactive spark plasma sintering.
Interfacial Ti reactions improve wetting and bonding between W and Cu.
Ti-assisted reactive sintering reduces surface oxides at W/Cu interfaces.
Improved wetting, bonding, and oxide removal mitigate void formation and phase segregation.
A continuous and robust interphase enhances thermal transport.
A continuous and robust interphase enhances mechanical integrity.
Relative to conventional infiltration or non-reactive SPS, Ti-assisted RSPS will produce lower porosity and a more uniform microstructure.
Relative to conventional infiltration or non-reactive SPS, Ti-assisted RSPS will improve thermal conductivity.
Relative to conventional infiltration or non-reactive SPS, Ti-assisted RSPS will improve mechanical durability under irradiation.
Standard SPS or infiltration W-Cu composites typically exhibit interfacial voids and phase separation.
The intervention is applicable under cyclic thermal loading and irradiation characteristic of fusion-reactor joints.
The optimal reactive-aid identity and concentration remain uncertain.
Long-term stability of the proposed graded interphase under extended irradiation has not been established.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as an already formed W skeleton or W-particle preform embedded in a Cu matrix, whereas the intervention is described as adding Ti to a mechanically alloyed W-Cu powder mixture. These are materially different feedstock configurations, and the hypothesis does not explain how one transitions to the other.
